claims.claim: Anger at wrongdoing can be good and even holy.

stances.summary: There is a just anger and an unjust one. Rage and revenge are vices, but the anger that rises to correct wrongdoing belongs to a good person, and God Himself has it.
stances.quote: But that anger which we may call either fury or rage ought not to exist even in man, because it is altogether vicious; but the anger which relates to the correction of vices ought not to be taken away from man; nor can it be taken away from God, because it is both serviceable for the affairs of men, and necessary.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7, 1886
stances.work: A Treatise on the Anger of God (De ira Dei)
stances.context: Written about 313-314 against the Epicureans (who said God cares for nothing) and the Stoics (who would uproot anger). Earlier in the same chapter: "But the Stoics did not see that there is a distinction between right and wrong, that there is a just and also an unjust anger; and because they did not find a remedy for the matter, they wished altogether to remove it." He defines just anger as "an emotion of the mind arousing itself for the restraining of faults". In chapter 21 he reads "Be angry, and sin not" as proof that God "did not tear up anger by the roots, but restrained it", forbidding only that we persevere in it. Important limit: his just anger is mainly for those in our charge. In Divine Institutes 6.19 he says anger is given "for restraining the faults of those who are in our power", so "as it is both just and necessary to employ anger towards the young, so it is both pernicious and impious to use it towards those of our own age." Most of the treatise is about God's anger, which he defends as necessary to His goodness and justice.

stances.summary: Christians do not ask whether a good person gets angry but why. Anger at a wrongdoer that aims to set him right is no fault, and even Christ felt indignation.
stances.quote: In our ethics, we do not so much inquire whether a pious soul is angry, as why he is angry; not whether he is sad, but what is the cause of his sadness; not whether he fears, but what he fears. For I am not aware that any right thinking person would find fault with anger at a wrongdoer which seeks his amendment
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 2, 1887
stances.original: Denique in disciplina nostra non tam quaeritur utrum pius animus irascatur, sed quare irascatur; nec utrum sit tristis, sed unde sit tristis; nec utrum timeat, sed quid timeat. Irasci enim peccanti ut corrigatur, contristari pro adflicto ut liberetur, timere periclitanti ne pereat nescio utrum quisquam sana consideratione reprehendat.
stances.work: The City of God (De civitate Dei)
stances.context: Book 9 dates from about 415-417. The Latin is from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ9.shtml). He is answering the Stoics, who counted such emotions as vices. The same chapter adds a qualification: perhaps feeling these emotions belongs to "the infirmity of this life", for "the holy angels feel no anger while they punish those whom the eternal law of God consigns to punishment", and God is said to be angry without any disturbance. In City of God 14.9 he argues that the citizens of God's city rightly fear, desire, grieve and rejoice, cites the "sorrowful indignation" of Christ at hard hearts, and says that while we live in this weakness "we are rather worse men than better if we have none of these emotions at all." Earlier (On the Sermon on the Mount 1.9, about 394) he read Matthew 5:22 as forbidding anger "without a cause", and later (Retractations 1.19.4) admitted the Greek manuscripts lack those words.

stances.summary: Anger is useful if used at the right time: not to avenge yourself, but to check people who do wrong. Most people get it backwards, furious when hurt themselves and cowardly when others are wronged.
stances.quote: What then is the proper time for anger? When we are not avenging ourselves, but checking others in their lawless freaks, or forcing them to attend in their negligence.
stances.translation: Sir George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 10, 1888
stances.work: Homilies on the Gospel of Matthew
stances.context: Preached at Antioch about 390. Just before: Christ "hath not altogether taken the thing away" because we cannot be free of passions, and "because this passion is even useful, if we know how to use it at the suitable time", citing Paul's anger at the Corinthians and Galatians. Just after: "But most men do the contrary; becoming like wild beasts when they are injured themselves, but remiss and cowardly when they see despite done to another: both which are just opposite to the laws of the Gospel. Being angry then is not a transgression, but being so unseasonably." He reads Matthew 5:22 with "without a cause". Elsewhere he is much more guarded: on Ephesians 4:26 (Homily 14 on Ephesians) he says "It were good indeed never to be angry", and treats "Be ye angry" as a concession to weakness. Several famous pro-anger lines under his name are NOT his (see misattributions: the Opus Imperfectum).

stances.summary: Anger from a bad temper and anger from zeal for good are different things. Zealous anger at sin is good: Phinehas was praised for it and Eli was punished for lacking it. It must stay the servant of reason.
stances.quote: For if there was no anger originating in virtue, Phinees would never have allayed the fierceness of God's visitation by his sword. Because Eli lacked such anger, he quickened against himself the stirrings of the vengeance of the Most High to an implacable force.
stances.translation: Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, Morals on the Book of Job, vol. 1 (Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1844), translator not named
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Iob)
stances.location: book 5, chapter 45, section 82 (on Job 5:2, "wrath killeth the foolish man")
stances.context: Written about 579-595. The same section says the anger "which hastiness of temper stirs is one thing, and that which zeal gives its character to is another. The first is engendered of evil, the second of good", and directly rejects the monastic reading of "Be angry and sin not": "Which doubtless they fail to interpret aright, who would only have us angry with ourselves, and not with others likewise, when they sin. For if we are bidden to love our neighbours as ourselves, it follows that we should be as angry with their erring ways as with our own evil practices." Section 83 limits it: zealous anger must "never gain dominion over the mind" but follow reason "like a handmaid", and even good zeal troubles contemplation for a while. His summary line: "Anger from zeal disturbs the wise, but anger from sin destroys the fool." In the Pastoral Rule (3.16) he warns hot-tempered rulers that they often "think the goad of their anger to be the zeal of righteousness", yet says a person is not full of the Spirit who "in the calm of meekness forsakes the fervour of zeal". This is the source Aquinas later used for "zealous anger".

stances.summary: Anger is a gift of the Creator. Stirred at the right time and in the right way it makes us brave and enduring, and it can serve good deeds, as with Phinehas and Samuel.
stances.quote: God forbid that we should turn into occasions for sin gifts given to us by the Creator for our salvation! Anger, stirred at the proper time and in the proper manner, is an efficient cause of manliness, patience, and endurance.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, excerpt translated in his Prolegomena, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Homily 10, Against the Angry (Homilia adversus iratos)
stances.location: section 6 (quoted in the Prolegomena to NPNF2 vol. 8, "The Homilies")
stances.context: The full homily is not translated in NPNF; Jackson quotes this passage (with an ellipsis) inside his summary, and I could not load the Greek to check it. Treat only the two quoted sentences as Basil's words: the rest of Jackson's excerpt ("Anger is to be used as a weapon ... The wrath of Phinehas was justifiable. So was the wrath of Samuel against Agag. Thus, anger very often is made the minister of good deeds") may be condensed. Most of the homily is a vivid attack on anger. In Letter 22 (on the monastic life) he lists among a Christian's duties that he ought not "to be angry", but "to convict the wrong-doer in season, not with the desire of his own vindication, but of his brother's reformation". The sheepdog image sometimes quoted from this homily was not verified.

stances.summary: Anger is not part of the soul itself, but like any passion it is a tool. Ruled by reason it becomes courage; aimed at the noble it deserves praise, as Phinehas' anger did.
stances.quote: But, whenever their impulse is towards what is noble, then they become matter for praise, as his desire did to Daniel, and his anger to Phineas, and their grief to those who nobly mourn.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: Gregory of Nyssa, On the Soul and the Resurrection (Macrina's words in her brother's dialogue)
stances.location: the discussion of the passions, about a third of the way through
stances.context: Written by Gregory of Nyssa about 380, after her death; her words are as he recorded them. Gregory first objects that "Phineas' anger pleased the Deity"; Macrina answers that passions "have not been allotted to human nature for any bad purpose at all" but become "instruments of virtue or of vice", like iron made into a sword or a ploughshare: under reason "anger fortitude"; and "If anger is to be extinguished, what arms shall we possess against the adversary?" She also insists anger and desire are not the soul's essence but "like warts growing out of the soul's thinking part", which the purified soul will lose.

stances.summary: When an opponent slandered his dead brother Basil, he answered in anger and defended it: anger on behalf of another, not oneself, can be right, and here meekness would have been the worse fault.
stances.quote: Perhaps, however, this suspicion about us will be disarmed by remembering that this display of anger is not on our own behalf, but because of insults levelled against our father in God; and that it is a case in which mildness would be more unpardonable than anger.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: Against Eunomius, prefatory Letter 1 to his brother Peter
stances.context: Written about 380-382. He admits "the flame of my heart-felt indignation burst out against this writer" and worries readers will think him a raw controversialist. In On the Making of Man 18.5 (379-380) he teaches the general principle: "if reason instead assumes sway over such emotions, each of them is transmuted to a form of virtue; for anger produces courage".

stances.summary: A good God must be angry at the wicked. Anger, indignation and jealousy are fitting responses to evil in God, and man has them after God's likeness.
stances.quote: All appliances He must needs use, because of all contingencies; as many sensations as there are causes: anger because of the wicked, and indignation because of the ungrateful, and jealousy because of the proud, and whatsoever else is a hinderance to the evil.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.work: Against Marcion
stances.context: About 207-208, in his Montanist period (later judged heterodox; never venerated as a saint). He is defending the Creator against Marcion, whose "good" god never takes offence. The passage is about God's anger; he adds that "it is owing to Him that man is also similarly affected in a way which is equally his own", though human anger is less perfect. In book 1 (chapter 26) he argues that a god who forbids sin must take offence at it: "if he is offended, he ought to be angry; if angry, he ought to inflict punishment." On Patience opens with his confession that he is unfit to write on patience, which fits his reputation for temper.

stances.summary: God is truly angry with those who do evil, and still good and merciful to those who love and fear Him.
stances.quote: You will say, then, to me, "Is God angry?" Yes; He is angry with those who act wickedly, but He is good, and kind, and merciful, to those who love and fear Him
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: To Autolycus
stances.context: Bishop of Antioch, writing about 180 to a pagan friend. About God's anger, not human anger. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: When heretics claimed him as one of theirs, he was angry and came down from the mountain to denounce them. Yet he told others not to be angry at a man who struck him, because the demon was to blame.
stances.quote: And once also the Arians having lyingly asserted that Antony's opinions were the same as theirs, he was displeased and wroth against them.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony
stances.context: Written by Athanasius, who knew him, soon after his death (about 357). This is Athanasius' approving narration of Antony's anger at heresy, not a teaching in Antony's own words; his recorded words there are "believe ye that the Creation itself is angry with them". In chapter 64, when a possessed youth struck him and his companions were angry, Antony said: "Be not angry with the young man, for it is not he, but the demon which is in him." So: anger at an insult to God's truth, never at a personal injury. Weak evidence; use with care.

stances.summary: Guard against anger first, and if it rises, keep it within bounds. But some things deserve anger: a person never moved by wickedness is not virtuous but merely slack.
stances.quote: The moral teacher who knew that the natural disposition should rather be guided by a reasonable course of teaching, than be eradicated, teaches morals, and says: "Be angry where there is a fault against which ye ought to be angry." For it is impossible not to be roused up by the baseness of many things;
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis ministrorum)
stances.context: Written about 388-391 for his clergy, closely modelled on Cicero. The sentence continues: "otherwise we might be accounted, not virtuous, but apathetic and neglectful." But the chapter opens "Let anger be guarded against. If it cannot, however, be averted, let it be kept within bounds. For indignation is a terrible incentive to sin", and the same section ends: "But he who wishes to prove his anger is righteous only gets the more inflamed, and quickly falls into sin." He also offers the monastic reading: "If ye are angry, be angry with yourselves". A deliberate middle view.

stances.summary: In his teaching, anger is human and ending it is Christian. In his own fights he defended furious indignation as zeal for God's honour, like Phinehas and Elijah.
stances.quote: I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, with G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.work: Letter 109, to Riparius (against Vigilantius)
stances.context: Letter 109 dates from 404. It goes on: "I have read of the javelin of Phinehas, of the harshness of Elijah, of the jealous anger of Simon the zealot ... There is no cruelty in regard for God's honour." The NPNF editor calls the letter "more noteworthy for its bitterness than for its logic". His moral teaching runs the other way. Letter 79.9 (400): "Just as anger is human and the repression of it Christian, so it is with other passions." Letter 130.13 to Demetrias (414): "For, if to be angry is human, to put an end to one's anger is Christian." His Commentary on Matthew (398), as quoted by Aquinas (Summa II-II q.158 a.1), says of Matthew 5:22: "Some codices add 'without cause.' However, in the genuine codices the sentence is unqualified, and anger is forbidden altogether." (Seen only in Aquinas; I did not load Jerome's Latin.) A strong candidate for the "argues with you" reveal on either side.

stances.summary: Anger at someone who wrongs you, even horribly, is always anger "without a cause". Anger at someone who tries to separate you from God is good.
stances.quote: but if a man wisheth to separate thee or to put "thee away from God, then to be angry and wroth with him "is a good thing.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: The Sayings of the Fathers (Budge's "Counsels of the Holy Men")
stances.context: The stray " marks inside the quote are Budge's running quotation marks at the start of each printed line; drop them for display. The full saying: a brother asks what "angry with his brother without a cause" means, and Poemen answers that if your brother oppresses, wrongs or defrauds you and you are angry, that is "without a cause"; even if he tears out your right eye or cuts off your right hand, anger at him is "without a cause"; only anger at one who would separate you from God is good. (The scan has an OCR error, "respedt", in the first half, so it is not quoted.) The Greek alphabetical collection has the same saying under Poemen; I did not check its wording. Elsewhere in Budge (saying 456) Poemen says "no monk should be a man of anger." The Sayings were written down in the late 5th century from oral tradition.

stances.summary: Anger has no place in a Christian's heart, which must be patient and never repay evil. But Christians must have zeal for the faith, like Phinehas, whose zeal pleased God.
stances.quote: We who have received the Spirit of God ought to have a jealousy for the divine faith; with such a jealousy as that wherewith Phineas both pleased God and justly allayed His wrath when He was angry, and the people were perishing.
stances.translation: Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: Epistle 72 (73 in modern numbering), To Jubaianus, on rebaptising heretics
stances.context: Both texts date from 256. The word is zeal ("jealousy"), not anger, but the example is Phinehas, the stock case of holy anger. In On the Advantage of Patience 16 he writes: "What shall I say of anger, of discord, of strife, which things ought not to be found in a Christian?", and a Christian "ought to admit neither anger nor discord within his breast, since he must neither return evil for evil, nor bear hatred." So: never anger for oneself, zeal for God's truth.

stances.summary: A pastor must sometimes show anger for a person's good without actually feeling it, as a doctor chooses a treatment. The display can help; the passion is not needed.
stances.quote: In some cases we must even be angry, without feeling angry, or treat them with a disdain we do not feel, or manifest despair, though we do not really despair of them, according to the needs of their nature.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 2, In Defence of His Flight to Pontus
stances.context: Written about 362, on the duties of a priest as a physician of souls. It treats anger as a pastoral tool to be worn, not an emotion to be indulged. Basil's Longer Rules 51 (as summarised by Jackson in NPNF2 vol. 8) make a similar point: the superior "is not angry with the sick, but fights with the disease".

stances.summary: Anger must be rooted out completely, even anger with a good reason. The goal of patience is not to be angry for good reasons but never to be angry at all. Its only right use is against our own sinful thoughts.
stances.quote: For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all.
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum)
stances.context: Written about 420-426 for monks in Gaul; he passes on the teaching of Evagrius. In 8.2 he reports and rejects the view that "it is not injurious if we are angry with the brethren who do wrong, since ... God Himself is said to rage"; in 8.4 God's anger is a figure of speech. On Ephesians 4:31 (8.5): "he excepts none whatever as necessary or useful for us." 8.6: righteous or unrighteous, anger blinds alike: "It makes no difference whether gold plates, or lead, or what metal you please, are placed over our eyelids". 8.21 argues "without a cause" in Matthew 5:22 was added "by those who did not think that anger for just causes was to be banished". 8.22: "we ought never to be angry at all, whether for good or bad reasons". The one exception (8.7): anger "against the lustful emotions of our heart". Conferences 16.7 (Abba Joseph): "we should reckon nothing more damaging than anger and vexation". Gregory the Great later rejected exactly this reading.

stances.summary: Anger by its nature is meant for fighting the demons. Turning it against human beings is against its nature; the demons do it to darken the mind.
stances.quote: The nature of anger is to fight the demons ... But the demons, dragging us back toward worldly desires, force anger, against its nature, to fight human beings, so that the mind is darkened, falls away from knowledge, and becomes a traitor to the virtues.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek (Guillaumont's text, Sources Chrétiennes 171, as transcribed on Luke Dysinger's site)
stances.original: Φύσις θυμοῦ τὸ τοῖς δαίμουσι μάχεσθαι καί ὑπὲρ ἡστινοσοῦν ἡδονῆς ἀγονίζεσθαι. Διόπερ ὁι μὲν ἄγγελοι τὴν πνευματικὴν ἡμῖν ἡδονὴν ὑποβάλλοντες καὶ τὴν ἐκ ταύτης μακαριότητα, πρὸς τοὺς δαίμονας τὸν θυμὸν τρέψαι παρακαλοῦσιν· ἐκεῖνοι δ' ἆυ πάλιν πρὸς τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἕλκοντες ἡμᾶς τὸν θυμὸν παρὰ φύσιν μάχεσθαι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις βιάζονται, ἵνα σκοτισθεὶς ὁ νοῦς καὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἐκπεσὼν προδότης γένηται τῶν ἀρετῶν.
stances.work: Praktikos (The Monk: A Treatise on the Practical Life)
stances.context: Written in the Egyptian desert about 390-399. Evagrius was condemned with Origenism in 553 (heterodox by later judgment), but his teaching on the eight thoughts shaped Cassian, Climacus and the whole monastic tradition. The page's English is Dysinger's own modern translation (not public domain; not copied here). The Greek on that page has transcription slips ("δαίμουσι", "ἀγονίζεσθαι", "ἆυ"); the omitted middle says the angels suggest spiritual pleasure and urge us to turn anger against the demons. Praktikos 21: the sun must not set on our anger, and nothing makes the mind a deserter like disturbed anger; 23: do not fight the person who hurt you in your thoughts. The only exception is anger at demons, never at people.

stances.summary: The Holy Spirit is peace of soul and anger is turmoil of heart, so nothing blocks the Spirit like anger. Anger was given to fight the serpent, and we misuse it on our neighbour.
stances.quote: If the Holy Spirit is called peace of soul, and is so, and anger is turmoil of heart, and is called so, then nothing so walls off His presence in us as anger.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek
stances.original: Εἰ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον εἰρήνη ψυχῆς καὶ ὁρίζεται, καὶ ὑπάρχει· ἡ δὲ ὀργὴ, ταραχὴ καρδίας καὶ ὑπάρχει καὶ λέγεται. Οὐκ οὖν οὐδὲν οὕτω τὴν αὐτοῦ παρουσίαν ἐν ἡμῖν, ὡς θυμὸς ὑποτειχίζειν πέφυκε.
stances.work: The Ladder of Divine Ascent (Klimax)
stances.location: Step 8, On freedom from anger and on meekness
stances.context: Written at Sinai about 600-650. The modern English (Lazarus Moore, 1959) is copyrighted, so this is my own rendering. The step opens by defining freedom from anger as "an insatiable longing for dishonour" (Ἀοργησία τοίνυν ἐστὶν ἔφεσις ἀτιμίας ἀκόρεστος, ὡς ἐν τοῖς κενοδόξοις εὐφημίας ἀπέραντος.). Step 26 gives the one right use: "Φύσει ὁ θυμὸς ἐν ἡμῖν κατὰ τοῦ ὄφεως, κεχρήμεθα δὲ αὐτῷ ἡμεῖς κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον." = "Anger is in us by nature against the serpent, but we have used it against our neighbour." He also notes that some seize on an apparently reasonable pretext for anger. Same tradition as Evagrius and Cassian.

stances.summary: Zeal against other people's sins is a sickness, not wisdom. Weep and pray for the sinner as Christ did, who was not angry with sinners.
stances.quote: A zealous man will never reach peace of mind. And he that is destitute of peace is also destitute of gladness. Peace of mind is called complete health, zeal is the contrary of peace.
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923)
stances.work: Mystic Treatises (the first series of his Ascetical Homilies)
stances.location: Treatise 50 in Wensinck's numbering, "Short sections ... in which is shown the injury caused by foolish zeal under the pretext of fear of God"
stances.context: Isaac of Nineveh wrote in Syriac in the late 7th century, a bishop of the Church of the East, venerated by the Orthodox. Wensinck's numbering differs from modern editions. The same treatise continues that zeal "is not counted among man as a form of wisdom, but as one of the illnesses of the soul" (the scan has a stray page number inside that sentence, so it is not quoted), and: "Pray on his behalf, that thou mayest resemble Christ, who was not angry with sinners but prayed on their behalf." In the Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence: "Love does not know how to be angry ; it is not indignant". He does allow that Elijah and Moses' Levites did right when God commanded zeal, in a different passage, but treats that as an exception by divine order.

stances.summary: The perfect Christian is not angry at all, not even with the "good" passions like zeal, because he loves God wholly and hates none of God's creatures.
stances.quote: Nor is he angry; for there is nothing to move him to anger, seeing he ever loves God, and is entirely turned towards Him alone, and therefore hates none of God's creatures.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.work: Stromata (Miscellanies)
stances.context: Written about 200-202 in Alexandria. This is his portrait of the "true gnostic", the mature Christian. He grants that such affections "when produced rationally, are good", yet says they are "inadmissible in the case of the perfect man", who does not share even in "high spirit, for it takes its place alongside of wrath; although some say that these are no longer evil, but already good." In Stromata 4.23: "God is impassible, free of anger". But in The Instructor 1.8 he defends God's punishing anger against those who ask "if the Lord loves man, and is good, is He angry and punishes?", calling reproof "the surgery of the passions of the soul". So: correction yes, the passion of anger no.

stances.summary: Scripture tells us not to be angry at all. God's "wrath" is a figure of speech for His corrective discipline, not a passion.
stances.quote: Besides, the Scripture, which tells us not to be angry at all, and which says in the thirty-seventh Psalm, "Cease from anger, and forsake wrath,"
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.work: Against Celsus
stances.context: Written about 248. The sentence goes on: Scripture "would not involve God in the same passion from which it would have us to be altogether free." The chapter opens by saying that Christians do speak of the wrath of God but deny it is a passion in Him: what is called God's wrath "is a means of discipline". The point about human anger is made in passing, while arguing about God. Several of Origen's other teachings were condemned in 553 (heterodox by later judgment).

stances.summary: A wrathful man is not acceptable even if he works miracles. Never go to sleep holding anger, or let anyone sleep holding anger against you.
stances.quote: If a man of wrath were to raise " the dead, he would not be accepted by any man.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: The Sayings of the Fathers (Budge's "Counsels of the Holy Men")
stances.context: The stray " mark is Budge's running quotation mark at a line start; drop it for display. Budge's Syriac says "by any man"; the Greek alphabetical collection has a version under Agathon that I did not check (it is usually cited as "acceptable to God"). Saying 347 (chapter 8): "I have never lain down to sleep and kept anger in my heart, or even a thought of enmity against any man; and I have never allowed any man to lie down to sleep keeping any anger against me." Agathon (4th century, Scetis) is not in the pool; his line is about the angry temperament in general rather than anger at wrongdoing.

stances.summary: Wrongdoers are sick in soul. They should be brought to justice with compassion, like a patient to a doctor, not with anger; the wise hate no one.
stances.quote: pity is rather due to the criminal, who ought to be brought to the judgment-seat by his accusers in a spirit not of anger, but of compassion and kindness, as a sick man to the physician, to have the ulcer of his fault cut away by punishment.
stances.translation: H. R. James, 1897 (Project Gutenberg)
stances.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
stances.context: Written in prison about 524, awaiting execution on charges he thought unjust. Spoken by Lady Philosophy, the book's voice of wisdom, to whom Boethius assents. She concludes: "for the wise no place is left for hatred; only the most foolish would hate the good, and to hate the bad is unreasonable." The Consolation is philosophical rather than overtly Christian.

stances.summary: It is not lawful to be angry, even when a wrong has been done to us; the memory of such things should be wiped from the mind.
stances.quote: since it is not lawful to be angry, all remembrance of such things, as it annoys us, ought to be blotted from our minds.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.work: Dialogues
stances.context: Written about 404 by the biographer of Martin of Tours, speaking in his own person in the dialogue (about a runaway freedman). His friend Gallus has just admitted of an angry acquaintance, "I will not indeed deny that he had just reasons for his wrath; but where the battle is hard, the crown of victory is all the more glorious." In the Life of Martin 27 he says of Martin: "No one ever saw him enraged". Not in the pool.

splits_fathers: Genuinely split, with strong voices on both sides, which makes this a good quiz item. For: the bishops and moralists who had to judge, correct and defend the faith. Lactantius wrote a whole book on just anger; Augustine ("not whether a pious soul is angry, but why"); Chrysostom (anger is for checking wrongdoers, not avenging yourself); Gregory the Great (anger from zeal versus anger from vice, Phinehas praised and Eli punished); Basil; Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina (anger under reason becomes courage). Tertullian and Theophilus defend God's anger at the wicked. In the middle: Ambrose (guard against it, yet be angry where there is a fault), Jerome (anger is human, ending it is Christian, yet his own letters rage for God's honour), Poemen (anger at wrongs done to you is always "without a cause"; anger at one who pulls you from God is good), Cyprian (no anger, but zeal like Phinehas), Gregory of Nazianzus (show anger as a medicine without feeling it). Against: the desert and monastic line Evagrius, Cassian, Climacus and Isaac, who say anger's only proper target is the demons or one's own sins, never another person ("not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all"); Clement's perfect Christian feels no anger; Origen, Agathon, Boethius and Sulpicius. The dividing line is explicit: Cassian rejects the "just cause" reading of Matthew 5:22, and Gregory the Great rejects Cassian's "be angry only with yourself" reading of Psalm 4:4. Almost all, on both sides, agree that anger for revenge, for money, or kept overnight is sinful, and that it must obey reason.
splits_people_today: Lopsided toward agree. Most people today, religious or not, accept "righteous anger" or moral outrage at injustice as healthy, and many Christians point to Jesus clearing the temple. A real minority says no: contemplative and Orthodox Christians formed by the desert tradition, people influenced by Buddhism or by Stoicism's current revival, some pacifists and nonviolence teachers, and many who have been hurt by other people's "righteous" anger; they would say grief, prayer and firm action without anger are better. The claim as worded will draw perhaps three quarters agreement. To split people better, sharpen it toward the Fathers' real dividing line, for example: "When someone does real wrong, the holiest response is anger at it" versus "A truly holy person grieves over wrongdoing but does not get angry", or separate anger at wrongs done to you (almost everyone among the Fathers says no) from anger at wrongs against God or others (where they split).

misattributions.line: He who is not angry, whereas he has cause to be, sins. For unreasonable patience is the hotbed of many vices, it fosters negligence, and incites not only the wicked but even the good to do wrong.
misattributions.truth: From the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 11, an anonymous 5th-century Latin commentary (by an Arian author) long printed among Chrysostom's works. Aquinas quotes it as Chrysostom (Summa II-II q.158 a.8); the New Advent edition of the Summa marks it "falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom". Often shortened online to "He who is not angry when he has cause, sins."

misattributions.line: He that is angry without cause, shall be in danger; but he that is angry with cause, shall not be in danger: for without anger, teaching will be useless, judgments unstable, crimes unchecked.
misattributions.truth: Same source, the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 11; quoted by Aquinas (Summa II-II q.158 a.1) and flagged there as falsely ascribed.

misattributions.line: Anger, when it has a cause, is not anger but judgment.
misattributions.truth: Same source, the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 11 (Summa II-II q.158 a.8).

misattributions.line: Hope has two beautiful daughters; their names are Anger and Courage. Anger at the way things are, and Courage to see that they do not remain as they are.
misattributions.truth: No source in Augustine's works is known; it circulates without any citation. A text search of the three NPNF Augustine volumes used here (vols. 1, 2 and 6) found nothing like it. Treat as unsourced and do not use.

notes: 1) The best head-to-head for the reveal: Gregory the Great against John Cassian. Cassian: "the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all." Gregory, answering exactly that school: "they fail to interpret aright, who would only have us angry with ourselves, and not with others likewise, when they sin." Chrysostom against Isaac makes a vivid East-East pair ("remiss and cowardly when they see despite done to another" against "A zealous man will never reach peace of mind"). 2) Poemen's saying is the most usable single item: it splits anger at wrongs done to me (never right) from anger at what separates me from God (good). A quiz may want two statements here. 3) Many "pro" Fathers still forbid anger over personal injury; Lactantius even limits just anger to correcting those in one's charge (children, pupils, servants), and calls anger at equals "pernicious and impious". 4) Several defenders speak of God's anger rather than human anger (Tertullian, Theophilus, Lactantius in part). Several opponents (Cassian, Origen, Clement) deny that God has anger as a passion. If the quiz wants a separate item on God's anger, the split is there. 5) Leads checked: Lactantius, On the Anger of God 17 and 21 hold; Basil's homily is verified only through Jackson's excerpt (section 6), and the sheepdog image was not found; Cassian Institutes 8 holds (and Conferences 16.7); Evagrius Praktikos 24 holds (On Prayer not checked); Gregory Moralia 5.45 holds and Pastoral Rule 3.16 holds; Chrysostom Homily 16 on Matthew holds, and the popular Chrysostom lines are the Opus Imperfectum; Augustine City of God 14.9 holds but 9.5 is the sharper text; Jerome's temper is documented in Letter 109; desert sayings: Agathon and Poemen found in Budge; "Ammonas" appears in Budge as "Abba Ammon", who prayed fourteen years to overcome anger (saying 257), a personal struggle rather than a position, so not recorded. 6) Not found or no position: Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Perpetua, Hippolytus (a Psalm fragment under his name says "God is without passion", attribution doubtful), Novatian, Hilary, Ephrem (the Nisibene hymn lines on anger are spoken by Satan, not Ephrem), Athanasius in his own voice, Syncletica, Moses the Black (Budge has him silent under insult, no teaching), Arsenius, Martin (only described as never angry), Paulinus, Benedict (Rule 4: "not to give way to anger", not checked in a public-domain text), Pelagius. 7) Every quote comes from a public-domain translation except Evagrius and Climacus (own renderings, Greek given). Public-domain quotes keep lower-case pronouns for God where the translator used them (for example "wroth", "his"); apply the site's capitals rule for display. 8) Every quote was checked by machine against the text at its url after collapsing whitespace. The ccel.org .txt files carry footnote markers like [147]; quotes were cut to avoid them.
